citation: Maryam Sorkhou, Eliza L Dent, Tony P George. Cannabis use and mood disorders: a systematic review. Frontiers in public health. 2024;12:1346207. doi:10.3389/fpubh.2024.1346207. PMID:38655516.
study_design: Systematic review
population: 78 cross-sectional and longitudinal studies involving major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, or general-population mood outcomes
exposure_intervention: Cannabis use or cannabis use disorder
comparator: Lower/no cannabis exposure or differing exposure as defined by included studies
outcome: Depressive and manic symptoms, incident mood disorder, prognosis, and treatment outcomes
main_result: Cannabis use was associated with more depressive and manic symptoms, greater likelihood of major depression or bipolar disorder, and less favorable prognosis in established mood disorders.
effect_estimate: NR
major_limitations: Mostly observational evidence with exposure heterogeneity and confounding; English-language restriction; association does not establish causation or temporal direction in every study.
individual_applicability: Supports treating cannabis as a clinically relevant modifier of mood course while preserving uncertainty about causation in one person.
quality_reason: Large systematic search and preregistration, but the abstract reports mainly qualitative observational synthesis.

citation: Mohammad Saad Javed, Rayane El-Khoury, Amr Ahmed Taha, Shuja Mohd Reagu. Prevalence of schizophrenia spectrum and bipolar disorder among patients with cannabis induced psychosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC psychiatry. 2026;26(1):186. doi:10.1186/s12888-025-07382-2. PMID:41664079.
study_design: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis
population: 13 studies, 7,515 people diagnosed with cannabis-induced psychosis
exposure_intervention: Cannabis-induced psychosis
comparator: Diagnostic outcomes within exposed cohorts
outcome: Later schizophrenia-spectrum or bipolar diagnosis
main_result: After cannabis-induced psychosis, pooled later diagnoses were approximately 20% schizophrenia spectrum and 5% bipolar disorder.
effect_estimate: Schizophrenia spectrum 20% (95% CI 15.8-29.5); bipolar disorder 5% (2.7-6.9)
major_limitations: Diagnostic transition can reflect initial misclassification or unmasked vulnerability; pooled unspecified outcomes were extremely heterogeneous.
individual_applicability: Reinforces the need for longitudinal observation during abstinence and euthymia to distinguish a transient substance state from an emerging primary disorder.
quality_reason: Focused quantitative review with quality appraisal, downgraded for diagnostic ambiguity and heterogeneous observational follow-up.

citation: Monika Luksaite, Tess Maguire, Jennifer Tarabay, Thomas Richardson. Positive beliefs about mania held by individuals with bipolar disorder: A systematic review. Psychology and psychotherapy. 2026;10.1111/papt.70087. doi:10.1111/papt.70087. PMID:42316899.
study_design: Systematic review with thematic synthesis
population: Studies of people with bipolar disorder reporting beliefs about hypomania or mania
exposure_intervention: Hypomanic or manic experiences
comparator: NR
outcome: Positive beliefs, including vitality, ability, achievement, creativity, and relationships
main_result: Five themes included enjoyable feelings, vitality, enhanced self/relationships, advanced ability and achievement, and creativity.
effect_estimate: NR
major_limitations: Predominantly qualitative, only perceptions rather than objective performance, and no evidence that any spiritual or personal interpretation is caused by mania.
individual_applicability: Shows that elevated states can alter perceived capability and meaning, warranting temporal clinical assessment without invalidating personal values.
quality_reason: Systematic methods and appraisal, but a small qualitative evidence base with indirect outcome.

citation: Marco Solmi, Marco De Toffol, Jong Yeob Kim, Min Je Choi, Brendon Stubbs, Trevor Thompson, et al. Balancing risks and benefits of cannabis use: umbrella review of meta-analyses of randomised controlled trials and observational studies. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2023;382:e072348. doi:10.1136/bmj-2022-072348. PMID:37648266.
study_design: Umbrella review of observational meta-analyses and randomized trials
population: 101 meta-analyses across general, clinical, and healthy populations
exposure_intervention: Cannabis, cannabinoids, and cannabis-based medicines
comparator: Non-use, placebo, or lower exposure as defined by source reviews
outcome: Psychosis, mania, cognition, psychiatric and central-nervous-system adverse events
main_result: Convincing observational evidence associated cannabis with psychosis (OR 1.71, 95% CI 1.47 to 2.00); cannabis also worsened positive psychotic symptoms and total psychiatric symptoms in experimental evidence, while cognition and mania signals were graded less consistently.
effect_estimate: Psychosis OR 1.71 (95% CI 1.47-2.00); positive psychotic symptoms equivalent OR 5.21 (3.36-8.01); total psychiatric symptoms 7.49 (5.31-10.42)
major_limitations: Umbrella synthesis inherits overlap, exposure heterogeneity, residual confounding, and variable quality of component reviews; it does not establish an individual's causal response.
individual_applicability: Directly relevant to cannabis as a state-risk modifier in people vulnerable to mental illness, but not proof that cannabis caused any reported episode.
quality_reason: Broad preregistered umbrella review with AMSTAR 2 and GRADE/credibility grading; important observational limitations remain.

individual_applicability: Supports monitoring for uncommon but serious state changes and possible agent/dose differences; it cannot attribute an episode to a stimulant in one patient.
quality_reason: Large preregistered review with formal appraisal and quantitative synthesis, substantially downgraded for heterogeneity and causal ambiguity.

citation: Shuichi Suetani, Faraz Honarparvar, Peter Muller, James P Kesby, Stephen Parker. Australasian psychiatry : bulletin of Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists. 2026;10398562261439662. doi:10.1177/10398562261439662. PMID:41916924.
study_design: Systematic review with synthesis without meta-analysis
population: Three heterogeneous studies of people with ADHD exposed to cannabis
exposure_intervention: Cannabis exposure in ADHD
comparator: People without ADHD and/or without cannabis exposure
outcome: Psychosis risk
main_result: The sparse available evidence did not show that cannabis-related psychosis risk is greater in people with ADHD than in people without ADHD; one study suggested a similar cannabis effect in both groups.
effect_estimate: NR
major_limitations: Only three heterogeneous studies; the absence of an ADHD-specific interaction is not evidence that cannabis is safe or that its baseline psychosis association is null.
individual_applicability: Qualifies, rather than negates, concern: ADHD has not been shown to multiply cannabis-associated psychosis risk beyond the general association.
quality_reason: Focused review and explicit bias assessment, but the evidence base is extremely small and heterogeneous.

citation: Kamilla W Miskowiak, Zacharias K Obel, Riccardo Guglielmo, Caterina Del Mar Bonnin, Christopher R Bowie, Vicent Balanzá-Martínez, et al. Efficacy and safety of established and off-label ADHD drug therapies for cognitive impairment or attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder symptoms in bipolar disorder: A systematic review by the ISBD Targeting Cognition Task Force. Bipolar disorders. 2024;26(3):216-239. doi:10.1111/bdi.13414. PMID:38433530.
study_design: Systematic review
population: 17 studies (N=2,136) of ADHD or pro-cognitive medications in bipolar disorder
exposure_intervention: Methylphenidate, amphetamine salts, modafinil-class drugs, bupropion, clonidine, or related agents
comparator: Placebo, baseline, or other treatment depending on study
outcome: ADHD symptoms, cognition, and treatment-emergent hypomania/mania
main_result: Some ADHD symptom benefit was observed; the review found no increased mania risk when stimulant treatment was used with mood stabilizers, while cognitive evidence was limited.
effect_estimate: NR
major_limitations: Small and heterogeneous studies, only five low-risk-of-bias studies, and limited cognitive outcomes; safety inference is conditional on mood stabilization.
individual_applicability: Counters a blanket claim that prescribed stimulants inevitably trigger mania; it does not establish safety for an unstabilized or individually vulnerable patient.
quality_reason: Task-force systematic review with independent review and design-specific bias appraisal, constrained by sparse primary evidence.

citation: Andreea Chiorean, Brett D M Jones, Mijia Murong, Christina Gonzalez-Torres, Stefan Kloiber, Abigail Ortiz, et al. Prescribed psychostimulants and other pro-cognitive medications in bipolar disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis of recurrence of manic symptoms. Bipolar disorders. 2024;26(5):418-430. doi:10.1111/bdi.13440. PMID:38670627.
study_design: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis
population: 27 studies; five studies quantitatively synthesized (n=1,653) in euthymic or depressed bipolar disorder
exposure_intervention: Psychostimulants or other pro-cognitive ADHD medications
comparator: Placebo
outcome: Young Mania Rating Scale and treatment-emergent manic symptoms
main_result: Medication exposure was not associated with higher mania ratings versus placebo (SMD -0.17, 95% CI -0.40 to 0.06), but heterogeneity was high and the authors described the evidence as preliminary.
major_limitations: Only five studies pooled, high heterogeneity, heterogeneous agents and designs, and selection of euthymic/depressed rather than acutely manic patients.
individual_applicability: Relevant to conditional risk under clinical treatment, not permission for unsupervised stimulant exposure or evidence against prior idiosyncratic activation.
quality_reason: Preregistered multi-database review with prospective and randomized designs, downgraded for sparse data and high inconsistency.

citation: Mohammad Saad Javed, Rayane El-Khoury, Amr Ahmed Taha, Shuja Mohd Reagu. Prevalence of schizophrenia spectrum and bipolar disorder among patients with cannabis induced psychosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC psychiatry. 2026;26(1):186. doi:10.1186/s12888-025-07382-2. PMID:41664079.
study_design: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis
population: 13 studies, 7,515 people diagnosed with cannabis-induced psychosis
exposure_intervention: Cannabis-induced psychosis
comparator: Diagnostic outcomes within exposed cohorts
outcome: Later schizophrenia-spectrum or bipolar diagnosis
main_result: After cannabis-induced psychosis, pooled later diagnoses were approximately 20% schizophrenia spectrum and 5% bipolar disorder.
effect_estimate: Schizophrenia spectrum 20% (95% CI 15.8-29.5); bipolar disorder 5% (2.7-6.9)
major_limitations: Diagnostic transition can reflect initial misclassification or unmasked vulnerability; pooled unspecified outcomes were extremely heterogeneous.
individual_applicability: Reinforces the need for longitudinal observation during abstinence and euthymia to distinguish a transient substance state from an emerging primary disorder.
quality_reason: Focused quantitative review with quality appraisal, downgraded for diagnostic ambiguity and heterogeneous observational follow-up.

citation: Cagatay Ermis, Antti Tanskanen, Olivier Corbeil, Johannes Lieslehto, Eduard Vieta, Christoph U Correll, et al. Reduced risk of cause-specific hospitalisations and all-cause hospitalisation/mortality during treatment with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder medications in the course of bipolar disorder: a Swedish registry-based within-subject cohort study. BMJ mental health. 2026;29(1):e302159. doi:10.1136/bmjment-2025-302159. PMID:41856665.
study_design: Registry-based within-subject cohort
population: 17,971 people in Sweden with bipolar disorder receiving ADHD medication, mean follow-up 8.9 years
exposure_intervention: Add-on ADHD medication during antipsychotic and/or mood-stabilizer treatment
comparator: Periods in the same individuals using antipsychotic/mood stabilizer without ADHD medication
outcome: Psychiatric, substance-related, somatic, mania-related, and all-cause hospitalization/mortality
main_result: Add-on stimulants were associated with lower psychiatric and substance-related hospitalization and were not associated with higher mania-related hospitalization (aHR 0.93, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.20).
effect_estimate: Psychiatric hospitalization aHR 0.89 (0.85-0.93); substance-related hospitalization 0.75 (0.70-0.81); mania-related hospitalization 0.93 (0.72-1.20)
major_limitations: Time-varying confounding, clinical selection, adherence and prescribing-channel bias, and hospitalization captures only severe outcomes; all exposure occurred in treated bipolar disorder.
individual_applicability: Important counterevidence to inevitable harm when ADHD medication follows mood stabilization, while not excluding short-lived activation or risk outside this context.
quality_reason: Large long-term within-person design reduces stable confounding but cannot remove time-varying treatment selection.

citation: Valerio Ricci, Thomas Fraccalini, Giovanni Martinotti, Giuseppe Maina. Cannabis cessation and neurocognitive recovery: Patterns, predictors, and clinical implications-a systematic review. The American journal on addictions. 2026;35(4):451-470. doi:10.1111/ajad.70156. PMID:41872072.
study_design: Systematic review with narrative synthesis
population: 26 studies of cannabis cessation, with abstinence from at least 72 hours to years
exposure_intervention: Cannabis cessation
comparator: Active use, earlier abstinence, or baseline
outcome: Cognition, neuroimaging, and biomarkers
main_result: Cognitive improvement often began within the first week, while some attention and executive deficits persisted beyond acute cessation; recovery varied with age of onset and exposure intensity.
effect_estimate: NR
major_limitations: Heterogeneous abstinence definitions, exposure histories and methods; narrative synthesis; persistence may reflect residual confounding or premorbid traits.
individual_applicability: Supports using a documented abstinence interval and repeated measurement rather than interpreting either immediate impairment or residual symptoms as definitive trait evidence.
quality_reason: Systematic search and design-appropriate appraisal, downgraded for heterogeneous narrative evidence and uncertain premorbid control.

citation: Eli Somer, Oren Herscu, Muthanna Samara, Hisham M Abu-Rayya. Maladaptive Daydreaming and Psychopathology: A Meta-Analysis. International journal of psychology : Journal international de psychologie. 2025;60(2):e70027. doi:10.1002/ijop.70027. PMID:39999955.
study_design: Meta-analysis of 40 studies
population: 24,977 participants across included studies; mean age 28.75 years
exposure_intervention: Operationalized maladaptive daydreaming across included studies; specific instruments NR in abstract
comparator: Lower maladaptive-daydreaming levels or comparison groups varied across studies
outcome: Loneliness, shame, emotion regulation, anxiety, depression, dissociation, ADHD, autism, trauma, compulsive and other psychopathology
main_result: Maladaptive daydreaming was positively associated with loneliness, shame, emotion-regulation difficulty, and broad psychopathology. The synthesis demonstrates comorbidity but does not establish escape function, temporal direction, or that alternatives fully explain MD.
effect_estimate: NR
major_limitations: Disorder-specific pooled estimates are absent from the abstract; The abstract does not describe temporal or experimental designs; Broad comorbidity cannot distinguish cause, consequence, or construct overlap; Emotional-compensation function was not directly tested
individual_applicability: Group-level associations cannot identify why one person daydreams or whether their experience is maladaptive.
quality_reason: Large focal meta-analysis supports association claims, but direction, function, construct distinctness, and effect magnitudes cannot be established from the abstract.

citation: Silvia Casale, Simon Ghinassi, Jon D Elhai. A 2-wave study on the associations between dissociative experiences, maladaptive daydreaming, bodily dissociation, and problematic social media use. Journal of behavioral addictions. 2025;14(3):1419-1428. doi:10.1556/2006.2025.00075. PMID:40932793.
study_design: Two-wave cross-lagged panel study over 4 months
population: 216 adults aged 18-33 years, 79.2% female
exposure_intervention: Problematic social-media use, maladaptive daydreaming, absorption, and bodily dissociation
comparator: Prior level of each construct in cross-lagged models
outcome: Later maladaptive daydreaming and dissociative experiences
main_result: Baseline problematic social-media use predicted later bodily dissociation and absorption; no other cross-lagged effects were detected, providing no positive directional finding for maladaptive daydreaming.
effect_estimate: PSMU to bodily dissociation β=0.15, p=0.005; PSMU to absorption β=0.13, p=0.026
major_limitations: Small, predominantly female convenience sample; Only two waves and four months of follow-up; Self-report constructs; The abstract does not state the MD-specific coefficient, only that no other cross-lagged effects occurred
individual_applicability: Does not determine the direction of one person's maladaptive daydreaming, but it weighs against claiming that direction is established.
quality_reason: Longitudinal temporal modeling is directly relevant, but the small two-wave sample and abstract-level null reporting limit confidence.

citation: Francesco Maria Boccaccio, Renata Rizzo, Concetta Pirrone, Jan K Buitelaar. Mapping the association between cognitive disengagement syndrome and internalizing disorders: A systematic scoping review with meta-analysis and meta-regression. Journal of affective disorders. 2026;412:122159. doi:10.1016/j.jad.2026.122159. PMID:42341946.
study_design: Systematic scoping review with three-level meta-analysis and meta-regression of 82 studies
population: Healthy and clinical children, adolescents, and adults with varying cognitive-disengagement-syndrome levels
exposure_intervention: Cognitive disengagement syndrome, a daydreaming and hypoarousal-related construct distinct from ADHD inattention
comparator: Lower CDS levels and statistical adjustment for ADHD inattention in included evidence
outcome: Depression, anxiety, broader internalizing symptoms, and limited functional outcomes
main_result: CDS had moderate-to-strong associations with internalizing outcomes that persisted after adjustment for ADHD inattention. Longitudinal evidence was stronger for later depression than anxiety; functional and symptom-overlap evidence was sparse.
effect_estimate: Depression r=0.56; anxiety r=0.46; broader internalizing r=0.44
major_limitations: CDS is not maladaptive daydreaming; Very few functional-outcome studies; Symptom overlap was not analytically addressed; Same-informant studies inflated effects and longitudinal evidence was scarce
individual_applicability: Highlights an alternative construct that requires measurement rather than assuming all daydreaming reflects MD or ADHD.
quality_reason: Meta-analytic estimates and ADHD-adjusted findings are strengths, downgraded for indirectness to MD, overlap concerns, and limited longitudinal function data.
